# Feminist Economics style: "percent" in running text (tables keep %); numbers under 100 spelled out in prose.
.numword <- function(n) {
  ones <- c("zero","one","two","three","four","five","six","seven","eight","nine","ten","eleven","twelve","thirteen",
            "fourteen","fifteen","sixteen","seventeen","eighteen","nineteen")
  tens <- c("", "", "twenty","thirty","forty","fifty","sixty","seventy","eighty","ninety")
  if (n < 20) return(ones[n + 1])
  if (n %% 10 == 0) return(tens[n %/% 10 + 1])
  paste0(tens[n %/% 10 + 1], "-", ones[n %% 10 + 1])
}
.inl <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("inline")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(inline = function(x) {
  x <- .inl(x)
  if (is.character(x)) x <- gsub("([0-9])\\\\?%", "\\1 percent", x)
  if (is.character(x) && length(x) == 1 && grepl("^[0-9]{1,2}$", x)) x <- .numword(as.integer(x))
  x
})

```{r analysis}
# ---- Person and household variables: all defined on pd BEFORE any subset ----
YES <- CODE$yes_no["yes"]; NO <- CODE$yes_no["no"]
pd[, `:=`(
  need_sc    = fcase(special_care == YES, 1L, special_care == NO, 0L, default = NA_integer_),
  need_child = as.integer(hh_n_under6 > 0),
  any_child  = as.integer(care_child > 0),
  any_adult  = as.integer(care_dep_adult > 0),
  any_emp    = as.integer(employment > 0),
  # Probable care recipient: unable to work owing to disability, or records
  # receiving personal or medical care from others on the diary day.
  recipient  = as.integer(pas %in% CODE$pas_disabled | receiving_care > 0),
  age_lc     = cut(age, c(14, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64, 74, Inf),
                   labels = c("15-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65-74", "75+"))
)]
# Caregiver availability is asked only when need_sc == 1 (Block 4, item 18).
pd[, carer_avail := fcase(need_sc == 1 & caregiver == YES, 1L,
                          need_sc == 1 & caregiver == NO, 0L, default = NA_integer_)]
pd[, `:=`(need_cg   = fcase(need_sc == 0, 0L, need_sc == 1 & carer_avail == 1, 1L,
                            need_sc == 1 & carer_avail == 0, 0L, default = NA_integer_),
          need_nocg = fcase(need_sc == 0, 0L, need_sc == 1 & carer_avail == 0, 1L,
                            need_sc == 1 & carer_avail == 1, 0L, default = NA_integer_))]
pd[, `:=`(hh_n_nonrec_women = sum(female == 1 & age >= 15 & recipient == 0),
          hh_n_recip = sum(recipient), hh_any_60 = as.integer(any(age >= 60))), by = hh_id]
pd[, no_woman := as.integer(hh_n_nonrec_women == 0)]
pd[, spouse_rec := recipient[match(spouse_pid, pid)]]
pd[, older_couple := as.integer(hh_size == 2 & hh_n_diarists == 2 & !is.na(spouse_pid) &
                                  age >= 60 & spouse_age >= 60)]

# A0: men and women 15+ with both need measures (households and shares).
# A : A0 without probable care recipients (all person-level carer analyses).
A0 <- pd[age >= 15 & sex %in% c("Men", "Women") & !is.na(need_sc) & !is.na(need_child)]
A0[, sex := droplevels(sex)]
A  <- A0[recipient == 0]

H <- unique(A0, by = "hh_id")
n_hh_sc <- sum(H$need_sc == 1)
pr_need_adult <- wmean(H$need_sc, H$weight)
pr_need_child <- wmean(H$need_child, H$weight)
pr_avail      <- wmean(H[need_sc == 1]$carer_avail, H[need_sc == 1]$weight)
pr_sc_60      <- wmean(H[need_sc == 1]$hh_any_60, H[need_sc == 1]$weight)
pr_60_sc      <- wmean(H[hh_any_60 == 1]$need_sc, H[hh_any_60 == 1]$weight)
pr_recip_flag <- wmean(H[need_sc == 1]$hh_n_recip > 0, H[need_sc == 1]$weight)
pr_nowoman    <- wmean(H[need_sc == 1]$no_woman, H[need_sc == 1]$weight)

# ---- Women's share of household care minutes, households with the need ------
hshare <- function(d, y) {
  h <- d[, .(f = sum(get(y) * female), t = sum(get(y)), w = weight[1]), by = hh_id][t > 0]
  wmean(h$f / h$t, h$w)
}
agg_share <- function(d, y) sum(d[[y]] * d$female * d$weight) / sum(d[[y]] * d$weight)
sh_child   <- hshare(A0[need_child == 1], "care_child")
sh_adult   <- hshare(A0[need_sc == 1], "care_dep_adult")
ag_child   <- agg_share(A0[need_child == 1], "care_child")
ag_adult   <- agg_share(A0[need_sc == 1], "care_dep_adult")
sh_adult_60  <- hshare(A0[need_sc == 1 & hh_any_60 == 1], "care_dep_adult")
sh_adult_n60 <- hshare(A0[need_sc == 1 & hh_any_60 == 0], "care_dep_adult")
sh_adult_cg  <- hshare(A0[need_sc == 1 & carer_avail %in% 1], "care_dep_adult")
sh_adult_ncg <- hshare(A0[need_sc == 1 & carer_avail %in% 0], "care_dep_adult")
sh_div4_sc   <- hshare(A0[need_sc == 1], "unpaid_care")

# ---- Means, participation and intensity conditional on need --------------------
gap <- function(d, y) est_gap(d, y, "sex", "Men", "Women")
g_cc_m <- gap(A[need_child == 1], "care_child"); g_ac_m <- gap(A[need_sc == 1], "care_dep_adult")
g_cc_p <- gap(A[need_child == 1], "any_child");  g_ac_p <- gap(A[need_sc == 1], "any_adult")
mcc <- est_mean(A[need_child == 1], "care_child", "sex")
mac <- est_mean(A[need_sc == 1], "care_dep_adult", "sex")
pcc <- est_mean(A[need_child == 1], "any_child", "sex")
pac <- est_mean(A[need_sc == 1], "any_adult", "sex")
dcc <- decompose_participation(A[need_child == 1], "care_child", "sex")
dac <- decompose_participation(A[need_sc == 1], "care_dep_adult", "sex")
mac0 <- est_mean(A[need_sc == 0], "care_dep_adult", "sex")
gv <- function(r, g) { x <- r$est[r$group == g]; if (length(x)) x else NA_real_ }
dv <- function(r, g, v) { x <- r[[v]][r$group == g]; if (length(x)) x else NA_real_ }

# ---- Linear combinations of coefficients (e.g. women's total response) -------
lincom <- function(m, terms, w = rep(1, length(terms))) {
  if (is.null(m) || !all(terms %in% names(coef(m)))) return(list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA))
  b <- sum(w * coef(m)[terms]); S <- vcov(m)[terms, terms, drop = FALSE]
  se <- sqrt(drop(t(w) %*% S %*% w))
  list(est = b, se = se, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(b / se)))
}

# ---- Need x gender interactions (Table 2) -------------------------------------
controls <- ctrl(A, c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "married", "urban", "i(mpce_quintile)",
                      "hh_size", "hh_n_60plus", "proxy_report"))
FE <- fe(A)
mreg <- function(y, d = A) reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~ female * need_sc + female * need_child +",
                                                  controls, FE)), d)
r_ac <- mreg("care_dep_adult"); r_cc <- mreg("care_child"); r_uc <- mreg("unpaid_care")
r_emp <- mreg("employment"); r_ft <- mreg("free_time"); r_sl <- mreg("sleep")
ac_fn <- coef_of(r_ac, "female:need_sc"); ac_n <- coef_of(r_ac, "need_sc")
ac_w  <- lincom(r_ac, c("need_sc", "female:need_sc"))
cc_fn <- coef_of(r_cc, "female:need_child"); cc_n <- coef_of(r_cc, "need_child")
cc_w  <- lincom(r_cc, c("need_child", "female:need_child"))
uc_w  <- lincom(r_uc, c("need_sc", "female:need_sc"))
emp_fn <- coef_of(r_emp, "female:need_sc"); emp_f_n <- coef_of(r_emp, "need_sc")
emp_w  <- lincom(r_emp, c("need_sc", "female:need_sc"))
ft_w   <- lincom(r_ft, c("need_sc", "female:need_sc"))
sl_w   <- lincom(r_sl, c("need_sc", "female:need_sc"))

# ---- Costs to working-age carers, by caregiver availability (Table 3) ---------
cost_ctrl <- c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "married", "urban", "i(mpce_quintile)",
               "hh_size", "hh_n_60plus", "hh_n_under6")
ce_fit <- function(y, d, rhs) reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~", rhs, "+", ctrl(d, cost_ctrl), fe(d))), d)
cost_y <- c(care_dep_adult = "Dependent-adult care (min)", unpaid_care = "All caregiving, Division 4 (min)",
            unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic work (min)", employment = "Employment (min)",
            any_emp = "Any employment on diary day (share)", employed = "Employed, usual status (share)",
            free_time = "Free time (min)", sleep = "Sleep (min)")
share_y <- c("any_emp", "employed")
Wn  <- A[female == 1 & age <= 64]
Mn  <- A[female == 0 & age <= 64]
Wn0 <- A0[female == 1 & age <= 64]   # including probable recipients (robustness)
fit_W  <- lapply(names(cost_y), function(y) ce_fit(y, Wn, "need_sc"))
fit_M  <- lapply(names(cost_y), function(y) ce_fit(y, Mn, "need_sc"))
fit_Wa <- lapply(names(cost_y), function(y) ce_fit(y, Wn, "need_cg + need_nocg"))
names(fit_W) <- names(fit_M) <- names(fit_Wa) <- names(cost_y)
cost_W   <- lapply(fit_W, coef_of, term = "need_sc")
cost_M   <- lapply(fit_M, coef_of, term = "need_sc")
cost_cg  <- lapply(fit_Wa, coef_of, term = "need_cg")
cost_ncg <- lapply(fit_Wa, coef_of, term = "need_nocg")
diff_av  <- lapply(fit_Wa, lincom, terms = c("need_cg", "need_nocg"), w = c(1, -1))
c_ac <- cost_W$care_dep_adult; c_emp <- cost_W$employment; c_ft <- cost_W$free_time
c_sl <- cost_W$sleep; c_empd <- cost_W$employed; c_dom <- cost_W$unpaid_domestic
c_emp_inc <- coef_of(ce_fit("employment", Wn0, "need_sc"), "need_sc")
c_ac_cg <- cost_cg$care_dep_adult; c_ac_ncg <- cost_ncg$care_dep_adult
c_emp_cg <- cost_cg$employment; c_emp_ncg <- cost_ncg$employment
d_ac_av <- diff_av$care_dep_adult; d_emp_av <- diff_av$employment
m_c_ac <- cost_M$care_dep_adult; m_c_emp <- cost_M$employment
n_W_ncg <- sum(Wn$need_nocg == 1, na.rm = TRUE)

# ---- Life-course profile of care, households with each need -----------------
lc <- function(d, y) rbindlist(lapply(c("Men", "Women"), function(s) {
  r <- est_mean(d[sex == s], y, "age_lc"); r$sex <- s; r
}))
lc_adult <- lc(A[need_sc == 1], "care_dep_adult")
lc_child <- lc(A[need_child == 1], "care_child")
lc_adult_w <- lc_adult[sex == "Women"][which.max(est)]
lc_adult_m <- lc_adult[sex == "Men"][which.max(est)]
lc_child_w <- lc_child[sex == "Women"][which.max(est)]
Wsc <- A[need_sc == 1]
tot_ac <- Wsc[, sum(care_dep_adult * weight)]
sh_min_60w <- Wsc[, sum(care_dep_adult * weight * (female == 1 & age >= 60))] / tot_ac
sh_min_60m <- Wsc[, sum(care_dep_adult * weight * (female == 0 & age >= 60))] / tot_ac
sh_min_60  <- sh_min_60w + sh_min_60m
g_old_ac <- gap(A[need_sc == 1 & age >= 60], "care_dep_adult")
g_old_ap <- gap(A[need_sc == 1 & age >= 60], "any_adult")

# ---- Spouses caring for spouses ----------------------------------------------
SC   <- A[need_sc == 1 & spouse_rec %in% 1]          # linked spouse is a probable recipient
SC60 <- SC[age >= 60]
n_sc_m <- sum(SC$female == 0); n_sc_w <- sum(SC$female == 1)
g_sc   <- gap(SC, "care_dep_adult"); g_scp <- gap(SC, "any_adult")
g_sc60 <- gap(SC60, "care_dep_adult")
msc  <- est_mean(SC, "care_dep_adult", "sex")
OCn  <- uniqueN(A0[older_couple == 1 & need_sc == 1]$hh_id)
OC   <- A[older_couple == 1 & need_sc == 1]
g_oc <- gap(OC, "care_dep_adult")

# ---- Men's care when no adult woman is present -------------------------------
M  <- A[need_sc == 1 & female == 0]
g_nw   <- est_gap(M, "care_dep_adult", "no_woman", 0, 1)
g_nwp  <- est_gap(M, "any_adult", "no_woman", 0, 1)
g_nwd  <- est_gap(M, "unpaid_domestic", "no_woman", 0, 1)
m_nw_men  <- wmean(M[no_woman == 1]$care_dep_adult, M[no_woman == 1]$weight)
WW <- A[need_sc == 1 & female == 1]
m_w_women <- wmean(WW$care_dep_adult, WW$weight)
n_nw_men <- sum(M$no_woman == 1)
r_nw <- reg(as.formula(paste("care_dep_adult ~ no_woman +",
                             ctrl(M, c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "married", "urban",
                                       "i(mpce_quintile)", "hh_size", "hh_n_60plus")), fe(M))), M)
g_nw_adj <- coef_of(r_nw, "no_woman")
men_close_gap <- isTRUE(is_pos(g_nw) && m_nw_men >= 0.75 * m_w_women)
men_above <- isTRUE(m_nw_men >= m_w_women)

# ---- Who provides adult care: relationship to head -------------------------
rel_lab <- c("1" = "Head", "2" = "Spouse of head", "3" = "Married child",
             "4" = "Child's spouse", "5" = "Unmarried child", "6" = "Grandchild",
             "7" = "Parent or parent-in-law", "8" = "Other relative", "9" = "Non-relative")
carers <- A[need_sc == 1 & care_dep_adult > 0 & !is.na(rel)]
who <- carers[, .(mins = sum(care_dep_adult * weight)), by = .(sex, rel)][, share := mins / sum(mins)]
who_w <- who[sex == "Women"][order(-share)]
top_rel <- function(k) if (nrow(who_w) >= k) tolower(rel_lab[as.character(who_w$rel[k])]) else "--"
dil_share <- sum(who[sex == "Women" & rel == CODE$relation["child_spouse"]]$share)
wife_share <- sum(who[sex == "Women" & rel %in% CODE$relation[c("head", "spouse")]]$share)
son_share <- sum(who[sex == "Men" & rel %in% CODE$relation[c("married_child", "unmarried_child")]]$share)
dil_top <- isTRUE(CODE$relation["child_spouse"] %in% head(who_w$rel, 2))

# ---- Relationship to the probable recipient (households with exactly one) ----
# Roster codes are relative to the head; map (carer code, recipient code) to the
# carer's relationship to the recipient. Linked spouses use spouse_pid directly.
rr_map <- function(c, r, is_sp) {
  out <- rep("Other relative or non-relative", length(c))
  set <- function(cond, v) out[cond & !is.na(cond)] <<- v
  set(r %in% c(1, 2) & c %in% c(3, 5), "Son or daughter")
  set(r %in% c(1, 2) & c == 4, "Son- or daughter-in-law")
  set(r %in% c(1, 2) & c == 6, "Grandchild")
  set(r %in% c(1, 2) & c == 7, "Parent")
  set(r == 7 & c == 1, "Son or daughter")
  set(r == 7 & c == 2, "Son- or daughter-in-law")
  set(r == 7 & c %in% c(3, 4, 5, 6), "Grandchild")
  set(r %in% c(3, 5) & c %in% c(1, 2), "Parent")
  set(r == 4 & c %in% c(1, 2), "Parent-in-law")
  set(r == 6 & c %in% c(3, 4, 5), "Parent")
  set(r == 6 & c %in% c(1, 2), "Grandparent")
  set(r %in% c(3, 5) & c %in% c(3, 5), "Sibling")
  set(is_sp, "Spouse")
  out
}
R1 <- pd[recipient == 1, .(n_rec = .N, rec_pid = pid[1], rec_rel = rel[1], rec_age = age[1],
                            rec_female = female[1]), by = hh_id][n_rec == 1]
C1 <- A[need_sc == 1 & !is.na(rel)][R1, on = "hh_id", nomatch = 0]
C1[, rr := rr_map(rel, rec_rel, !is.na(spouse_pid) & spouse_pid == rec_pid)]
n_hh_r1 <- uniqueN(C1$hh_id)
who_r <- C1[care_dep_adult > 0, .(mins = sum(care_dep_adult * weight)), by = .(sex, rr)][, share := mins / sum(mins)]
rrs <- function(sx, r) sum(who_r[sex == sx & rr %in% r]$share)
dil_r <- rrs("Women", "Son- or daughter-in-law"); son_r <- rrs("Men", "Son or daughter")
dau_r <- rrs("Women", "Son or daughter"); sil_r <- rrs("Men", "Son- or daughter-in-law")
wsp_r <- rrs("Women", "Spouse"); msp_r <- rrs("Men", "Spouse")
# Older recipients (60+) separately: the case the patrilineal-care literature addresses
who_r60 <- C1[care_dep_adult > 0 & rec_age >= 60, .(mins = sum(care_dep_adult * weight)), by = .(sex, rr)][, share := mins / sum(mins)]
dil_r60 <- sum(who_r60[sex == "Women" & rr == "Son- or daughter-in-law"]$share)
son_r60 <- sum(who_r60[sex == "Men" & rr == "Son or daughter"]$share)
dil_gt_son_r <- isTRUE(dil_r60 > son_r60)
n_hh_r1_60 <- uniqueN(C1[rec_age >= 60]$hh_id)

# ---- Sandwich: women 35-54 facing both needs --------------------------------
Wm <- A[female == 1 & age >= 35 & age <= 54]
Wm[, both := as.integer(need_sc == 1 & need_child == 1)]
r_sw <- reg(as.formula(paste("unpaid_care ~ both + need_sc + need_child +",
                             ctrl(Wm, c("i(edu_tier)", "married", "urban", "i(mpce_quintile)", "hh_size")),
                             fe(Wm))), Wm)
sw_tot <- coef_of(r_sw, "both")
pr_both <- wmean(Wm$both, Wm$weight)

more_gendered_adult <- isTRUE(sh_adult > sh_child)
emp_cost <- is_neg(c_emp)
avail_more <- isTRUE(is_pos(d_ac_av))
avail_less <- isTRUE(is_neg(d_ac_av))
ok <- function(e) isTRUE(!is.null(e$est) && !is.na(e$est))
likely <- function(e, more = "more", less = "less")
  if (ok(e)) paste(diff_pp(e, more, less), "likely") else "[not estimable] in their likelihood"
women_dominate <- isTRUE(sh_adult >= 0.6)
wives_dil_main <- isTRUE(wsp_r + dil_r > 0.35)
dil_gt_son <- dil_gt_son_r
old_carers_big <- isTRUE(sh_min_60 >= 0.25)
adult_near_child <- isTRUE(sh_adult >= sh_child - 0.05)
need_q_valid <- isTRUE(gv(mac0, "Women") < 0.2 * gv(mac, "Women"))
recip_matters <- isTRUE(abs(c_emp_inc$est - c_emp$est) > c_emp$se)
sc_small <- min(n_sc_m, n_sc_w) < 30
nw_small <- n_nw_men < 30
```

\begin{abstract}
Population averages of care time mix the gender division of care with differences in who lives with someone who needs it. India's Time Use Survey 2024 asks each household whether a member needs special care and records a diary for every member aged six and above. Where a child under six is present, women provide `r pctx(sh_child, 0)` of childcare minutes; where a member needs special care, they provide `r pctx(sh_adult, 0)` of dependent-adult care minutes. Conditional on household characteristics, need is associated with higher adult-care time: by `r f1(ac_w$est)` minutes a day (SE `r f1(ac_w$se)`) for women and `r f1(ac_n$est)` (SE `r f1(ac_n$se)`) for men`r iff(is_sig(c_emp), paste0(", and working-age women's paid work by ", f1(c_emp$est), " minutes"), "; working-age women's paid work is not detectably different")`. `r iff(is_pos(g_nw), iff(men_close_gap, "Men's adult-care time reaches women's average only when no adult woman is present. ", "Even when no adult woman is present, men care far less than women do. "), "")``r iff(women_dominate, "Family long-term care in India is provided mostly through women's time.", "Long-term care policy may consider who in the household provides care.")`
\keywords{care work, eldercare, long-term care, gender, time use, India}
\jel{J14, J16, J22}
\end{abstract}

# Introduction {#sec:s1}

Care for people who cannot fully look after themselves is the core of the unpaid economy [@folbre1994pays; @folbre2006measuring; Addati, Cattaneo, Esquivel, and Valarino -@addati2018care]. Its largest component in most countries is childcare, and the time-use literature has studied parental care intensively [@sayer2004parents; @craig2011share; Folbre, Yoon, Finnoff, and Fuligni -@folbre2005measure]. Care of sick, frail and disabled adults has received much less attention, especially outside high-income countries, even though demand for it is rising fastest. India's population aged 60 and above is growing faster than the population as a whole, co-residence with adult children remains the dominant living arrangement for older Indians, and a substantial share of them report difficulty with basic activities of daily living [International Institute for Population Sciences, National Programme for Health Care of Elderly, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, and University of Southern California -@iips2020lasi; @unfpa2023ageing]. Public and market provision of long-term care is still developing [@unfpa2023ageing; @who2015ageing], so most of this care is provided inside the household, by its members, without pay.

This paper asks a question that the Indian evidence has rarely addressed directly: *when a household needs care, who in it provides that care, and at what cost?* Population-wide comparisons of care time by sex [@hirway2011understanding; @nso2020tus] confound two things: the gender division of care within households that need it, and differences between men and women in whether they live in such a household. A man who records no care because no one in his household needs it and a man who records none while his wife nurses his mother both contribute zero to the male average. The same averaging hides the cost of care. Because only a minority of households need adult care on any day, its effect on women's paid work and leisure is diluted when the comparison is made across all households.

India's Time Use Survey 2024 [@nso2025tus] allows the two to be separated. Its household schedule asks whether any member aged five or above needs special care and, if so, whether a caregiver is available among household members. The survey also lists every member and records a 24-hour diary for each member aged six and above, so the time of every potential carer is observed together with the household's need. I use these questions to compare childcare in households with a child under six with care of dependent adults in households with a member who needs special care, and to estimate what that need costs women in paid work, free time and sleep.

Five results stand out. First, in households that need each type of care, women provide `r pct(sh_child, 0)` of household childcare minutes and `r pct(sh_adult, 0)` of dependent-adult care minutes; `r iff(more_gendered_adult, "adult care is, if anything, more feminized than childcare", "adult care is somewhat less feminized than childcare, but remains predominantly women's work")`. Women in such households are `r likely(g_ac_p)` than men in the same kind of household to record any adult care on the diary day. Second, conditional on age, education, consumption, household size and composition, state and day of the week, a household need for special care is associated with higher adult-care time for women, by `r est_se(ac_w)` and for men by `r est_se(ac_n)`. For women aged 15 to 64 it is associated with `r diff_txt(c_emp)` time in employment and `r diff_txt(c_ft)` free time. Third, `r iff(avail_more, "the cost depends on the household's own assessment of whether a caregiver is available: women's adult-care time rises more where a caregiver is reported available, consistent with that caregiver usually being a woman", iff(avail_less, "the cost depends on the household's own assessment of whether a caregiver is available: women's adult-care time rises less where a caregiver is reported available", "women's adult-care time responds similarly whether or not the household reports a caregiver available; the difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero"))`. Fourth, `r pct(sh_min_60, 0)` of all dependent-adult care minutes in need households are provided by people aged 60 and above`r iff(old_carers_big, ", so the care profile over the life course is not the one implied by the image of a \"sandwich generation\" alone", "")`. Fifth, `r iff(is_pos(g_nw), "men's care rises when no adult woman is present in the household, so men's low care time in mixed households reflects in part the presence of women to whom care is assigned", iff(ok(g_nw), "men's care does not rise measurably when no adult woman is present in the household, which points to care from outside the household or unmet need rather than male substitution", "few men live in need households without an adult woman, so men's substitution for women cannot be measured reliably"))`.

The paper contributes to three literatures. For feminist economics of care, it measures care conditional on need, which separates the gender division of care from household demography, and it uses the survey's own assessment of caregiver availability, a direct if coarse measure of the household's care capacity [@folbre2006measuring; @razavi2007political; @addati2018care]. For the economics of informal caregiving, which comes mostly from Europe and North America [@lilly2007labor; @heitmueller2007chicken; @vanhoutven2013informal; @bauer2015impacts], it provides diary-based evidence from a setting where co-residence is the norm, formal care is scarce, and women's attachment to paid work is already weak. For the study of gender and family structure in India, it documents how patrilocal residence and the expectation that daughters-in-law serve their husband's parents translate into minutes of care [@dyson1983kinship; @kandiyoti1988bargaining; @lamb2000white; @jayachandran2015roots].

# Care, need and gender: theory and evidence {#sec:s2}

## Care as work, responsibility and relationship

Feminist economics has argued for three decades that care is work, that it is unequally distributed by gender, and that its invisibility in national accounts and economic models has consequences for policy [@folbre1994pays; @himmelweit1995discovery; @folbre2001invisible]. Three features of care distinguish it from other unpaid work. First, care is a relationship with a person, not only a set of tasks: its quality depends on attention and continuity, and it involves emotional as well as physical labor [@tronto1993moral; @folbre2000love; @england2005emerging]. Second, care involves responsibility and availability. A carer who must remain within earshot of a frail parent is constrained even when not performing a recorded task, which is why time-use researchers distinguish active from passive or supervisory care [@folbre2004family; @folbre2006measuring]. Third, as @kittay1999love argues, those who do dependency work, caring for someone who cannot care for themselves, become dependent in turn: on a partner's earnings, on kin or on the state.

These features explain why care is gendered and why the gendering is persistent. @folbre1994pays analyzes the "structures of constraint" (assets, rules, norms and preferences) that assign the costs of caring for dependants disproportionately to women. Care motivated partly by affection and obligation is difficult to price, and those who provide it may be reluctant to withdraw it even when the terms are unfair, a feature that weakens their bargaining position [@folbre2001invisible; @england2005emerging]. The household is not a unit with a single welfare function but a site of "cooperative conflict" in which perceived contributions and fallback positions shape the division of work [@sen1990gender; @agarwal1997bargaining].

Care is also organized across institutions. @daly2000concept define social care as the activities and relations involved in meeting the physical and emotional needs of dependent adults and children, and the normative, economic and social frameworks within which they are assigned. @razavi2007political describes a "care diamond" of family, market, state and community, whose weights vary across countries and over time. In India, the state's main care infrastructure is directed at young children, through the anganwadi system, which is staffed largely by women workers; paid domestic work fills some of the gap for better-off households; and care of adults is expected to come from family members [@palriwala2010care]. The policy agenda that follows from this literature has been summarized as recognizing, reducing and redistributing unpaid care work [@elson2017recognize], extended to rewarding and representing care workers [@addati2018care]. All three Rs require measurement of who provides care and to whom.

## Measuring care with time-use data

Time-use diaries are the main instrument for measuring unpaid care [@budlender2010time; @charmes2019unpaid]. The International Classification of Activities for Time-Use Statistics (ICATUS) 2016 places unpaid caregiving for household members in its own major division, separate from unpaid domestic services, and distinguishes care of children, care of dependent adults and help to non-dependent adult household members [@un2016icatus].

Three measurement problems have been central to the feminist critique of diary data. First, diaries record activities, not responsibilities. Supervisory care and being "on call" are under-recorded unless they are probed, so care time measured as a primary activity is a lower bound on the time constrained by care [@folbre2004family; @folbre2006measuring]. Second, care is frequently done alongside other activities, so the primary-activity measure understates its extent and the intensity of the carer's work [@floro1995women]. Third, the diary day is a single day. Daily averages correctly estimate the population mean but mix people who never care with people who care every day; the participation rate on a given day understates the share of people who ever provide care, and conditional means overstate its usual intensity [@frazis2012think].

A less discussed problem matters most for this paper. Comparisons of care by sex across the whole population depend on who lives with a care recipient. Global compilations show women doing about three-quarters of unpaid care work [@charmes2019unpaid; @addati2018care], but they rarely condition on the presence of someone who needs care. For childcare, the age of the youngest child provides a natural conditioning variable, and studies routinely condition on it [@craig2011share; @sayer2004parents]. For adult care, the recipient is harder to identify, because adults who need help are not defined by age, and most surveys do not ask. Without a measure of need, low male care time cannot be distinguished from low male exposure to need.

## Informal care of adults and labor supply

A large literature, almost entirely from high-income countries, estimates the labor-market cost of caring for an adult. @lilly2007labor review this evidence and conclude that carers on average are not much less likely to be employed than non-carers, but that intensive carers are more likely to withdraw from work or reduce hours. Studies that address the endogeneity of caring find that treating it as exogenous overstates its employment effect, and that the effect is concentrated among co-resident and intensive carers [@heitmueller2007chicken]. European panel data show that care reduces employment and hours of work among people aged over 50 [@bolin2008next], with sizeable effects of intensive caregiving on mature women's employment that vary across countries with their care regimes [@crespo2014caregiving]. Reviews add costs to carers' mental and physical health [@bauer2015impacts; @coe2009caring], which are larger for women carers, partly because women face more care stressors [@pinquart2006gender].

Three features of this literature limit what it says about India. It defines carers by self-report of caregiving, so the counterfactual is a non-carer in any household, and selection into caring is the main identification problem. It studies settings where formal long-term care, pensions and women's employment are far more developed, so the margins of adjustment differ. And it mostly studies care of parents by adult children who live separately, whereas in India co-residence is the norm, and the carer is often a daughter-in-law rather than a daughter.

## Gender, kinship and care over the life course

Gerontology has long documented that family care of frail older people is provided mostly by women, above all by wives and daughters [@stone1987caregivers]. Middle-aged women carrying responsibilities to both older parents and their own children became "women in the middle" [@brody1981women] or the "sandwich generation" [@miller1981sandwich]. Two qualifications to this picture are important here. First, a substantial share of care for older people is provided by older people themselves, mainly spouses, and in later life men become a large group of carers, mostly for their wives [@arber1989men; @arber1991gender]. The gender gap in care is therefore not constant over the life course. Second, men's low care time in middle age may reflect the availability of women in the household rather than an absolute absence of male caring. Both qualifications are testable with diary data that cover every member of the household.

In South Asia, obligations to care are shaped by patrilineal and patrilocal kinship. @dyson1983kinship contrast the northern Indian kinship system, with village exogamy and patrilocal residence that separate women from their natal kin, with the southern system, in which women retain more contact with natal kin and more autonomy. @kandiyoti1988bargaining describes the "patriarchal bargain" of classic patriarchy: a young bride enters her husband's household subordinate to its senior women, and her position improves with age, through sons and through authority over her own daughters-in-law. Ethnographic work on aging in northern India describes the expectation that sons, and in practice their wives, provide *seva* (service and care) to aging parents in return for having been raised [@lamb2000white]. These accounts imply that the daughter-in-law is the expected carer of her husband's parents, and that care of the old is, in this sense, part of the marriage contract.

Demographic change is putting pressure on these arrangements. Falling fertility reduces the number of potential carers per older person, migration separates adult children from their parents, and rising life expectancy, longer for women than for men, increases the number of older widows [@rajan1999india; @unfpa2023ageing]. Disability is concentrated at older ages [@nso2019disability; @iips2020lasi]. At the same time, India's female labor-force participation is low by international standards and fell for married women between the mid-2000s and the early 2010s [@afridi2018married; @klasen2015stagnation; @chatterjee2018indian]. Explanations emphasize norms, the structure of labor demand, and household responsibilities [@fletcher2017women; @jayachandran2021social]. Extended-family structure has been shown to be associated with women's employment [@dhanaraj2019family], but the role of care of adults within that structure has not been measured directly. If care of the old is part of what keeps married women out of paid work, the coming increase in the old-age dependency ratio will make it harder to raise women's employment.

# Conceptual framework {#sec:s3}

Consider a household with members $i = 1, \dots, n$ who allocate their time among paid work, unpaid care, other unpaid work, leisure and sleep. The household's need for care of a dependent member, $S_h$, raises the total care time the household must supply. How that requirement is divided depends on each member's opportunity cost of time, on bargaining power, and on norms that assign care to particular positions in the household [@folbre1994pays; @sen1990gender; @agarwal1997bargaining]. In a unitary model with comparative advantage, the member with the lowest market wage supplies care, and since women's wages and employment opportunities are lower, women supply most of it. A bargaining or identity model gives the same prediction for a different reason: care is assigned by gender and position, and departures from the assignment are costly. The models differ in what they predict when the person to whom care is assigned is absent: comparative advantage predicts that the next-lowest-cost member takes over, while strong positional norms predict that care may go unmet or be bought in.

The framework implies four questions that the data can answer.

*Q1. Division conditional on need.* In households with each need, what share of care time do women provide, and how much of the population gender gap in care is a gap in exposure to need? If women's share of care in need households is similar to their share in the population, low male care is not a matter of exposure.

*Q2. Response and cost.* How much more care time do men and women record where there is need, and which other uses of time are lower? Paid work is the most-studied margin, but free time and sleep may adjust instead, particularly for women outside the labor force.

*Q3. Capacity.* The survey asks whether a caregiver is available among household members. A "no" answer can mean that no member is able to care, that the members who could care are occupied with paid work, or that the recipient is cared for from outside the household or not at all. If availability largely reflects the presence of a woman who can be assigned care, women's care time will rise more where a caregiver is reported available. If unavailability reflects strain, the women in those households may bear larger costs per carer.

*Q4. Position and life course.* Which members of the household supply care, by relationship to the head, sex and age? The kinship literature predicts a central role for daughters-in-law; the gerontological literature predicts a large role for spouses at older ages, and a smaller gender gap among older people. Men's care in households where no adult woman is present tests whether men's low care elsewhere reflects substitution by women.

# Data and measurement {#sec:s4}

## The Time Use Survey 2024

The Time Use Survey (TUS) 2024 was conducted by India's National Statistics Office between January and December 2024 [@nso2025tus]. It follows the 2019 survey [@nso2020tus], which asked a single combined question on whether a member needing special care lacked a caregiver and has been used to study women's unpaid work and care [e.g. @neetha2024participation]; I use the 2024 round because it separates need from caregiver availability, and compare the care shares with 2019 at the end of Section \ref{sec:s6}. The survey covers rural and urban India with a stratified multistage design in which first-stage units (villages and urban blocks) are the primary sampling units. Every member of a sampled household aged six and above reports, in a face-to-face interview, the activities of the 24 hours from 4 a.m. on the day before the interview, coded to ICATUS 2016. More than one activity can be recorded in a time slot, each flagged as major or minor. I use all `r fn(V$n_rows)` activity records, covering `r fn(V$n_diarists)` diaries in `r fn(V$n_households)` households and `r fn(V$n_fsu)` first-stage units. Time is aggregated to the person-day from major activities, so that all but `r fn(V$n_diaries_not1440)` of the `r fn(V$n_diarists)` diaries sum to exactly 1,440 minutes (Appendix Table \ref{tab:validation}). The roster lists `r fn(V$n_roster_6plus)` persons aged six and above; `r fn(V$n_roster_only_age6plus)` of them have no diary records in the file, which leaves the `r fn(V$n_diarists)` diaries, and the `r fn(V$n_third_gender)` diaries of third-gender respondents are excluded from the comparisons of women and men. All estimates use the survey multipliers, and standard errors are clustered on the first-stage unit.

## Need for care

*Need for special care* is the household's answer to the question "Is there any member (age 5+) who needs special care?" (Block 4, item 17 of the household schedule). The question does not restrict need to adults or to old age, and does not record the type or severity of need or the identity of the recipient. I therefore refer to it as special-care need, not eldercare need. `r pct(pr_need_adult, 1)` of households report such a need (`r fn(n_hh_sc)` households in the analysis sample). Of these, `r pct(pr_sc_60, 0)` include a member aged 60 or above`r iff(isTRUE(pr_sc_60 > 0.5), ", so most of the need is likely to concern older people", "")`; some recipients will be working-age adults or children aged 5 to 17 with a disability. Among households with a member aged 60 or above, `r pct(pr_60_sc, 1)` report a member needing special care.

*Caregiver availability* is the answer to "Is there any care giver available among household members?" (item 18), asked only when item 17 is "yes". `r pct(pr_avail, 0)` of households with a special-care need report a caregiver available. I interpret a "no" as an indicator of constrained care capacity, not as the absence of care: such households may draw on non-resident kin, neighbors or paid help, or care may be provided by members who do not consider themselves available.

*Need for childcare* is the presence of a child under six. Children under six do not keep diaries; their number is recovered as household size minus the number of diarists. `r pct(pr_need_child, 0)` of households have a child under six. Children aged five may appear in both need measures, which affects few households.

## Care and its recipients

Childcare is ICATUS 411--419 (physical care, medical care, teaching, talking and reading, playing, minding, and arrangements with schools and childcare providers) plus accompanying own children (442). Dependent-adult care is 421--429 (help with activities of daily living, medical care, administration, emotional support, passive care, and arrangements with care providers) plus accompanying dependent adults (443). Help to non-dependent adult household members (431--439) is excluded from both. Because the recipient of special care may be a child aged 5 to 17, care for whom is coded as childcare, I also report results for all caregiving in ICATUS Division 4.

The person who needs special care also keeps a diary. Including recipients among potential carers would bias the estimates: recipients do little care and little paid work because of the condition that makes them need care, so a household's need would appear to reduce women's employment partly through the employment of the women who need care. The survey does not identify the recipient. I flag as *probable recipients* members whose usual principal activity status is "not able to work owing to disability" and members who record receiving personal or medical care from others on the diary day (ICATUS 941--949). In `r pct(pr_recip_flag, 0)` of households with a special-care need at least one member is flagged. Probable recipients are excluded from all person-level analyzes of carers. The flag is deliberately broad: it also removes some people who visited a doctor, which makes the carer sample slightly more selected toward healthy members but does not affect the household-level shares of care, to which recipients contribute almost nothing.

## Samples

The household-level analysis uses all men and women aged 15 and above in households with non-missing answers to the need questions (`r fn(nrow(A0))` persons). The person-level analysis excludes probable recipients (`r fn(nrow(A))` persons), and the analysis of costs restricts it further to women and men aged 15 to 64. Transgender respondents are too few for separate estimates and are excluded.

Women's share of household care is computed for each household with positive care of the relevant type as the ratio of women's to all members' minutes, and averaged with household weights. I also report the aggregate ratio of women's to all care minutes. The two differ because the household-level average gives equal weight to households with little and much care.

```{r tab-desc}
row <- function(need, out, m, w) data.frame(Need = need, Outcome = out, Men = m, Women = w)
d1 <- rbind(
  row("Child under six", "Childcare, minutes per day", f1(gv(mcc, "Men")), f1(gv(mcc, "Women"))),
  row("Child under six", "Any childcare on diary day", pct(gv(pcc, "Men")), pct(gv(pcc, "Women"))),
  row("Child under six", "Minutes among those who provide childcare", f1(dv(dcc, "Men", "mean_doers")), f1(dv(dcc, "Women", "mean_doers"))),
  row("Child under six", "Women's share of household childcare", "", pct(sh_child)),
  row("Child under six", "Women's share of all childcare minutes", "", pct(ag_child)),
  row("Member needs special care", "Dependent-adult care, minutes per day", f1(gv(mac, "Men")), f1(gv(mac, "Women"))),
  row("Member needs special care", "Any dependent-adult care on diary day", pct(gv(pac, "Men")), pct(gv(pac, "Women"))),
  row("Member needs special care", "Minutes among those who provide adult care", f1(dv(dac, "Men", "mean_doers")), f1(dv(dac, "Women", "mean_doers"))),
  row("Member needs special care", "Women's share of household adult care", "", pct(sh_adult)),
  row("Member needs special care", "Women's share of all adult-care minutes", "", pct(ag_adult)),
  row("Member needs special care", "Women's share of household Division 4 care", "", pct(sh_div4_sc)),
  row("No member needs special care", "Dependent-adult care, minutes per day", f1(gv(mac0, "Men")), f1(gv(mac0, "Women"))))
tab(d1, caption = paste0("Care provided in households that need it, ages 15+", syn_note()), label = "desc",
    align = c("l", "l", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Survey-weighted. Persons aged 15+, excluding probable care recipients for person-level rows. ",
                   "Household share: ratio of women's to all members' minutes in households with positive care of that type, averaged with household weights. ",
                   "Aggregate share: women's minutes over all minutes. Division 4: all unpaid caregiving for household members (ICATUS 4xx)."))
```

# Empirical approach {#sec:s5}

The descriptive comparisons answer Q1. For Q2, I estimate for persons aged 15 and above

$$ y_{ih} = \alpha + \beta_1 W_i + \beta_2 S_h + \beta_3 W_i S_h + \beta_4 C_h + \beta_5 W_i C_h + X_{ih}'\gamma + \mu_{s} + \delta_{d} + \varepsilon_{ih}, $$

where $y_{ih}$ is minutes of an activity on the diary day for person $i$ in household $h$, $W_i$ indicates a woman, $S_h$ a household member needing special care, $C_h$ a child under six, $X_{ih}$ age band, education, marital status, urban residence, consumption quintile, household size, the number of members aged 60 and above, and whether the diary was reported by proxy, and $\mu_s$ and $\delta_d$ are state and day-of-week fixed effects. $\beta_2$ is men's response to need and $\beta_2 + \beta_3$ women's, which I report with its standard error.

For the costs to women and Q3, I estimate separately for women and men aged 15 to 64

$$ y_{ih} = \alpha + \theta^{A} S^{A}_h + \theta^{N} S^{N}_h + X_{ih}'\gamma + \mu_{s} + \delta_{d} + \varepsilon_{ih}, $$

where $S^{A}_h$ and $S^{N}_h$ indicate a special-care need with and without a caregiver reported available, the reference group is households with no such need, and $X_{ih}$ adds the number of children under six. The pooled version replaces the two indicators with $S_h$. Outcomes include minutes of dependent-adult care, all caregiving, domestic work, employment, free time and sleep, and two shares: any employment on the diary day and employment in the usual principal status. The last is the most direct labor-supply measure, since it refers to the year before the survey rather than to one day.

These coefficients are conditional associations, not causal effects. Households in which someone needs care are likely to be older, and may be poorer, than other households, and women in them may differ in unobserved ways from other women. The controls absorb the most important observable differences, including the number of older members, which separates the association with need from that with an older household. Two features of the setting limit the most common bias in the caregiving literature, selection into caring: need is measured at the household level, so the comparison is between women in households with and without need rather than between carers and non-carers, and in co-residential households the decision to care is arguably less a separate choice than a consequence of residence. Selection into co-residence remains: families may move a frail parent in with the child best able to care, or a daughter-in-law may withdraw from the labor market before need arises. I return to this in Section \ref{sec:s7}.

For Q4, I report the distribution of dependent-adult care minutes by the carer's sex and relationship to the head, the age profile of care by sex, and two comparisons: care by spouses of probable recipients, and men's care in need households with and without a non-recipient woman aged 15 or above.

# Results {#sec:s6}

## The division of care conditional on need

Table \ref{tab:desc} gives the core comparison. In households with a child under six, women aged 15 and above average `r f0(gv(mcc, "Women"))` minutes of childcare a day and men `r f0(gv(mcc, "Men"))`. Women are `r likely(g_cc_p)` than men to record any childcare. In households with a member who needs special care, women average `r f1(gv(mac, "Women"))` minutes of dependent-adult care and men `r f1(gv(mac, "Men"))`, a gap of `r est_se(g_ac_m)`. `r pct(gv(pac, "Women"))` of women and `r pct(gv(pac, "Men"))` of men in these households record some adult care on the diary day`r iff(!is.na(dv(dac, "Men", "mean_doers")), paste0(", and those who do spend ", f0(dv(dac, "Women", "mean_doers")), " and ", f0(dv(dac, "Men", "mean_doers")), " minutes respectively"), paste0("; women who do spend ", f0(dv(dac, "Women", "mean_doers")), " minutes"))`. In households with no special-care need, women record `r f1(gv(mac0, "Women"))` and men `r f1(gv(mac0, "Men"))` minutes of adult care`r iff(need_q_valid, ", which confirms that the need question identifies the households where adult care is concentrated", ", so a substantial amount of adult care takes place in households that do not report a special-care need")`.

Measured as women's share of household care minutes, `r iff(more_gendered_adult, "adult care is more feminized than childcare", "adult care is less feminized than childcare")`: `r pct(sh_adult, 0)` against `r pct(sh_child, 0)`. The aggregate shares, which weight households by the amount of care they provide, are `r pct(ag_adult, 0)` and `r pct(ag_child, 0)`. Counting all caregiving for household members, so that care of a disabled child recorded as childcare is included, women provide `r pct(sh_div4_sc, 0)` of care in households with a special-care need. `r iff(women_dominate, "Conditioning on need does not narrow the gender gap in care: differences in exposure to need explain little of women's dominance of care.", "Conditioning on need reveals substantial male participation in adult care that population averages hide.")`

The degree of feminization differs with the likely recipient. In need households that include a member aged 60 or above, women provide `r pct(sh_adult_60, 0)` of adult-care minutes; in need households with no member aged 60 or above, where the recipient is a working-age adult or an older child, `r pct(sh_adult_n60, 0)`. It also differs with care capacity: women provide `r pct(sh_adult_cg, 0)` of adult-care minutes where a caregiver is reported available and `r pct(sh_adult_ncg, 0)` where none is.

## Care time and need

```{r tab-reg, results="asis"}
reg_table(Filter(Negate(is.null), list("Adult care" = r_ac, "Childcare" = r_cc, "All care" = r_uc,
                                       "Employment" = r_emp, "Free time" = r_ft, "Sleep" = r_sl)),
          title = paste0("Care need, gender, and time use (minutes per day)", syn_note()), label = "tab:reg",
          keep = c("%^female$", "%need_sc", "%need_child"),
          dict = c(female = "Woman", need_sc = "Member needs special care", need_child = "Child under six",
                   "female:need_sc" = "Woman x special-care need", "female:need_child" = "Woman x child under six"),
          notes = paste("Persons 15+, excluding probable care recipients. All care: ICATUS Division 4.",
                        "Controls: age band, education, marital status, urban, consumption quintile, household size,",
                        "members 60+, proxy report; state and day-of-week fixed effects. Survey-weighted; FSU-clustered SEs."))
```

Table \ref{tab:reg} estimates how care time differs with need, by gender. Because adult care is almost absent in households without a special-care need (Table \ref{tab:desc}) and the controls barely shift it, the need coefficients in column 1 are close to the raw means in need households; I checked that this is not a coding artefact (the raw means are `r f2(gv(mac, "Men"))` and `r f2(gv(mac, "Women"))`, the coefficients `r f2(ac_n$est)` and `r f2(ac_w$est)`). In column 1, a household need for special care is associated with `r est_se(ac_n)` more dependent-adult care for men and an additional `r est_se(ac_fn)` for women, so that the total difference for women is `r est_se(ac_w)`. In column 2, a child under six is associated with `r est_se(cc_n)` more childcare for men and `r est_se(cc_w)` for women. Column 3 shows that the special-care difference is `r iff(isTRUE(uc_w$est > ac_w$est + 1.96 * ac_w$se), "larger", "similar")` when all caregiving is counted (`r est_se(uc_w)` for women), `r iff(isTRUE(uc_w$est > ac_w$est + 1.96 * ac_w$se), "so part of the care for special-care recipients is recorded as childcare or help to non-dependent adults", "so little of the difference is recorded under other care categories")`.

Columns 4 to 6 show how other activities differ. The need for special care is associated with `r diff_txt(emp_f_n)` employment for men and `r diff_txt(emp_w)` for women. Women's free time changes by `r est_se(ft_w)` and their sleep by `r est_se(sl_w)`. `r leis <- is_neg(ft_w) || is_neg(sl_w); iff(is_neg(emp_w) && leis, "Women in need households do less paid work and have less free time or sleep.", iff(is_neg(emp_w), "Women in need households mainly do less paid work.", iff(leis, "Women in need households have less free time and sleep, rather than less paid work.", "Within the precision of these estimates, no single use of time is clearly lower; the difference is spread across activities.")))`

## The cost to women and the role of caregiver availability

```{r tab-cost}
cell <- function(e, y) {
  if (is.null(e) || is.na(e$est)) return("--")
  d <- if (y %in% share_y) 3 else 1
  paste0(.fmt(e$est, d), stars(e$p), " (", .fmt(e$se, d), ")")
}
ct <- data.frame(
  Outcome = unname(cost_y),
  `Any need` = mapply(cell, cost_W, names(cost_y)),
  `Carer available` = mapply(cell, cost_cg, names(cost_y)),
  `No carer` = mapply(cell, cost_ncg, names(cost_y)),
  `(2) - (3)` = mapply(cell, diff_av, names(cost_y)),
  `Any need ` = mapply(cell, cost_M, names(cost_y)),
  check.names = FALSE)
names(ct)[2:6] <- paste0(names(ct)[2:6], " (", 1:5, ")")
names(ct)[5] <- "Difference (4)"
tab(ct, caption = paste0("Special-care need and the time use of women and men aged 15--64", syn_note()),
    label = "cost", align = c("l", rep("r", 5)),
    notes = paste0("Each cell is the coefficient (SE) on the need indicator(s) from a separate survey-weighted regression; ",
                   "reference group: households with no member needing special care. Columns (2) and (3) come from one regression with both indicators; ",
                   "column (4) is (2) minus (3). Probable care recipients excluded. Controls: age band, education, marital status, ",
                   "urban, consumption quintile, household size, members 60+, children under six; state and day-of-week fixed effects. ",
                   "FSU-clustered SEs. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01.")) |>
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Women" = 4, "Men" = 1))
```

Table \ref{tab:cost} focuses on working-age women and men. Among women aged 15 to 64, a household member needing special care is associated with `r diff_txt(c_ac)` dependent-adult care, `r diff_txt(c_dom)` domestic work, `r diff_txt(c_emp)` employment, `r diff_txt(c_ft)` free time and `r diff_txt(c_sl)` sleep. The probability of being employed in the usual principal status is `r diff_pp(c_empd)`. For men of the same age, the corresponding changes are `r diff_txt(m_c_ac)` adult care and `r diff_txt(m_c_emp)` employment.

When probable recipients are kept in the sample, the employment coefficient for women is `r est_se(c_emp_inc)` rather than `r est_se(c_emp)`. `r iff(recip_matters && isTRUE(c_emp_inc$est < c_emp$est), "Ignoring the recipient overstates the employment cost of care, because it counts the recipient's own absence from work as a cost to carers.", iff(recip_matters, "Excluding recipients makes the estimated employment cost larger, not smaller.", "The recipients' own low employment does not drive the estimate."))` The employment estimates differ in sign across samples: `r est_se(emp_w)` for women aged 15 and above in Table \ref{tab:reg}, `r est_se(c_emp)` for women aged 15 to 64, and `r diff_pp(c_empd)` in the usual-status employment rate. All are small, and their signs disagree, so I read them together as showing no consistent association between household care need and women's paid work, and certainly not as evidence that care raises it.

The second and third columns split need by whether the household reports a caregiver available. Where a caregiver is available, women's adult care rises by `r est_se(c_ac_cg)`; where none is available, by `r est_se(c_ac_ncg)`. The difference is `r est_se(d_ac_av)` and `r sig_phrase(d_ac_av$p)`. `r iff(avail_more, "The pattern is consistent with availability meaning, in practice, the presence of a woman to whom care can be assigned: where she exists, she provides it, and where she does not, the household reports no caregiver and less care is recorded.", iff(avail_less, "Women in households without an available caregiver provide more care, not less, consistent with the answer signalling strain on the women who care rather than the absence of care.", "The availability answer does not separate households with very different levels of women's care, so it should be read as a coarse indicator of capacity rather than as a measure of whether care is provided."))` For employment, the coefficients are `r est_se(c_emp_cg)` with a caregiver available and `r est_se(c_emp_ncg)` without (difference `r est_se(d_emp_av)`). The estimates for households without an available caregiver rest on `r fn(n_W_ncg)` women and are correspondingly imprecise.

These averages combine households with very different levels of need. The survey does not record severity, and the diary records one day. As in high-income countries [@lilly2007labor; @carmichael2003opportunity], the burden is likely to be concentrated among a minority of intensive carers whose costs are well above the mean.

## Who provides adult care

```{r tab-who}
rr_lev <- who_r[, .(t = sum(share)), by = rr][order(-t)]$rr
wt <- data.frame(`Carer's relationship to the recipient` = rr_lev,
  Women = pct(sapply(rr_lev, function(r) rrs("Women", r))),
  Men = pct(sapply(rr_lev, function(r) rrs("Men", r))),
  `Women, recipient 60+` = pct(sapply(rr_lev, function(r) sum(who_r60[sex == "Women" & rr == r]$share))),
  `Men, recipient 60+` = pct(sapply(rr_lev, function(r) sum(who_r60[sex == "Men" & rr == r]$share))),
  check.names = FALSE)
tab(wt, caption = paste0("Distribution of dependent-adult care minutes by carer's sex and relationship to the probable recipient", syn_note()),
    label = "who", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Need households with exactly one probable recipient (", fn(n_hh_r1), " households; ", fn(n_hh_r1_60), " with a recipient aged 60+). Shares of all adult-care minutes in each sample, summing to 100% over the women and men columns. Relationship to the recipient is derived from both members' relationship to the head (for example, the head's wife caring for the head's parent is a daughter-in-law); 'son or daughter' includes a head caring for a parent, who may be a son-in-law. Carers 15+, excluding probable recipients. Survey-weighted."))
```

```{r tab-who-head, eval = FALSE}
rl <- sort(unique(who$rel))
wt <- data.frame(
  `Relationship to head` = rel_lab[as.character(rl)],
  Women = pct(sapply(rl, function(r) sum(who[sex == "Women" & rel == r]$share))),
  Men   = pct(sapply(rl, function(r) sum(who[sex == "Men" & rel == r]$share))),
  check.names = FALSE)
wt <- wt[order(-sapply(rl, function(r) sum(who[rel == r]$share))), ]
tab(wt, caption = paste0("Distribution of dependent-adult care minutes by carer's sex and relationship to head", syn_note()),
    label = "who", align = c("l", "r", "r"),
    notes = "Share of all adult-care minutes in households with a special-care need (sums to 100% over both columns). Carers 15+, excluding probable recipients. Survey-weighted.") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "4.2cm") |> kableExtra::column_spec(2:3, width = "2.6cm")
```

Table \ref{tab:who} distributes adult-care minutes by the carer's relationship to the person who needs care. The survey does not name the recipient, so I restrict this analysis to the `r fn(n_hh_r1)` need households with exactly one probable recipient and derive each carer's relationship to that person from both members' relationship to the head. Wives caring for husbands provide `r pct(wsp_r, 0)` of adult-care minutes and husbands caring for wives `r pct(msp_r, 0)`. Daughters- and sons-in-law, almost all of them daughters-in-law, provide `r pct(dil_r, 0)`, sons and daughters `r pct(son_r + dau_r, 0)` (sons `r pct(son_r, 0)`, daughters `r pct(dau_r, 0)`). Where the recipient is aged 60 or above, daughters-in-law provide `r pct(dil_r60, 0)` of care minutes and sons `r pct(son_r60, 0)`. `r iff(dil_gt_son, "Under patrilineal norms the duty of caring for aging parents is assigned to the son; in these data the daughter-in-law carries out more of it", "Sons provide at least as large a share as daughters-in-law, which is not the pattern the ethnographic literature on patrilineal care obligations leads one to expect")` [@lamb2000white; @kandiyoti1988bargaining]. The derivation is approximate: the probable-recipient flag is imperfect, and a head caring for a parent-in-law is counted as a child.

## Care over the life course

```{r fig-lifecourse, fig.cap=paste0("Care by age and sex of the carer, in households with each type of need", syn_note(), ". Survey-weighted means with 95\\% confidence intervals; persons aged 15+, excluding probable care recipients."), fig.height=3.4, fig.width=7}
pl <- rbind(cbind(lc_adult, care = "Dependent-adult care\n(households with a member needing special care)"),
            cbind(lc_child, care = "Childcare\n(households with a child under six)"))
pl[, `:=`(lo = pmax(est - 1.96 * se, 0), hi = est + 1.96 * se,
          group = factor(group, levels = levels(pd$age_lc)))]
ggplot(pl, aes(group, est, color = sex, linetype = sex, shape = sex, group = sex)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.15, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ care, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey10", "grey50"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Age of carer", y = "Minutes per day")
```

Figure \ref{fig:fig-lifecourse} shows the age profile of care. Childcare in households with a child under six peaks for women aged `r lc_child_w$group``r iff(isTRUE(lc_child_w$group %in% c("15-24", "25-34", "35-44")), ", the ages of mothers of young children", "")`; at ages 55 to 64, women provide `r f0(lc_child[sex == "Women" & group == "55-64"]$est)` minutes, much of it presumably grandmothers' care of grandchildren. Women's dependent-adult care in households with a special-care need peaks at ages `r lc_adult_w$group` and men's at `r lc_adult_m$group`. People aged 60 and above provide `r pct(sh_min_60, 0)` of all adult-care minutes in need households (older women `r pct(sh_min_60w, 0)`, older men `r pct(sh_min_60m, 0)`). Among people aged 60 and above in these households, women provide `r diff_txt(g_old_ac)` adult care than men, and are `r likely(g_old_ap)` to provide any. `r iff(isTRUE(abs(g_old_ac$est) < abs(g_ac_m$est) - 1.96 * g_old_ac$se), "The gender gap in adult care is smaller in old age than over the whole adult life course, as the gerontological literature on spousal care predicts.", "The gender gap in adult care does not narrow measurably in old age, unlike the pattern documented for spousal care in high-income countries.")`

`r iff(isTRUE(pr_both < 0.05), "The \"sandwich generation\" facing both needs at once is a small group. ", "")`Women aged 35 to 54 facing both a child under six and a member needing special care are `r pct(pr_both, 1)` of women of that age. Their total caregiving is `r diff_txt(sw_tot)` than predicted by the two needs separately (`r sig_phrase(sw_tot$p)`). `r iff(is_neg(sw_tot), "The negative interaction means that the two needs do not add up: women facing both provide less care than the sum of the two separate associations, consistent with a ceiling on the time one woman can give or with care being shared with other members. Given how small the group is, the estimate says little about the population as a whole.", iff(is_pos(sw_tot), "The positive interaction means that the two needs compound: women facing both provide more care than the two separate associations imply.", "The interaction is not statistically distinguishable from zero, so the two needs appear to add up roughly."))`

## Spouses caring for spouses

The probable-recipient flag allows a closer look at spousal care. Among married persons in need households whose linked spouse is a probable recipient (`r fn(n_sc_w)` wives and `r fn(n_sc_m)` husbands), wives provide `r f1(gv(msc, "Women"))` minutes of adult care a day and husbands `r f1(gv(msc, "Men"))`, a gap of `r est_se(g_sc)` (`r sig_phrase(g_sc$p)`), and wives are `r likely(g_scp)` than husbands to provide any (`r sig_phrase(g_scp$p)`). Restricted to carers aged 60 and above, the gap is `r est_se(g_sc60)`. In the `r fn(OCn)` need households consisting only of an older couple, where the only possible household carer is the spouse, the gap is `r est_se(g_oc)`. `r iff(is_neg(g_sc) || is_pos(g_sc), iff(is_pos(g_sc), "Even when it is their spouse who needs care, husbands are less likely than wives to provide it, and the minutes gap, though less precisely estimated, points the same way.", "When it is their spouse who needs care, husbands provide more of it than wives."), "When it is their spouse who needs care, husbands are less likely than wives to provide any, but the gap in minutes is imprecise and not statistically significant at the 5% level, and among older couples living alone it disappears, consistent with the role of men as spousal carers documented in other settings.")` `r iff(sc_small, "These comparisons rest on few spouse carers and should be read as indicative.", "")` For older couples living on their own, the question of who cares has only one answer within the household.

## Men's care when no woman is present

Men's care depends on whether a woman is present to provide it. `r pct(pr_nowoman, 1)` of households with a special-care need contain no non-recipient woman aged 15 or above. `r iff(ok(g_nw), paste0("Men in such households (", fn(n_nw_men), " in the sample) provide ", diff_txt(g_nw), " dependent-adult care than men in need households with a woman present, and are ", likely(g_nwp), " to provide any. With controls, the difference is ", est_se(g_nw_adj), ". They also do ", diff_txt(g_nwd), " domestic work. Men in households without a woman provide ", f1(m_nw_men), " minutes of adult care a day, against ", f1(m_w_women), " for women in need households. ", iff(is_pos(g_nw), iff(men_close_gap, iff(men_above, "When there is no woman to assign care to, men's adult care is at or above women's average in need households, so men's low care elsewhere is consistent with care being assigned to women rather than with men's inability to provide it; the comparison rests on a small sample, and men caring alone may also face greater need.", "When there is no woman to assign care to, men's adult care approaches women's average, consistent with care being assigned to women rather than with men's inability to provide it."), "Men take on more care when there is no woman to provide it, but still far less than women do, which suggests that some care goes unmet or is provided from outside the household."), "Men's care does not rise measurably in households without a woman, which suggests that care in these households is provided from outside, by non-resident kin or paid help, or goes unmet."), iff(nw_small, " The comparison rests on few men and is indicative only.", "")), paste0("Men in such households number only ", fn(n_nw_men), " in the sample, too few for a reliable comparison."))`

## Comparison with 2019

The 2019 round asked only whether a member aged five or above needed special care and had no caregiver available, so the need-conditional comparisons cannot be repeated. The care shares can. Among persons aged 15 and above, women provided `r pct(cmp("03", "women_share_adultcare_all", 2019)$est, 0)` of all dependent-adult care minutes in 2019 and `r pct(cmp("03", "women_share_adultcare_all", 2024)$est, 0)` in 2024, and `r pct(cmp("03", "women_share_childcare_u6hh", 2019)$est, 0)` and `r pct(cmp("03", "women_share_childcare_u6hh", 2024)$est, 0)` of childcare in households with a child under six [@nso2020tus; @nso2025tus]. `r iff(isTRUE(cmp("03", "women_share_adultcare_all", 2024)$est >= cmp("03", "women_share_adultcare_all", 2019)$est), "Women's share of adult care rose and their share of childcare changed little, so the gender division of care did not become more equal between the two rounds.", "Women's share of adult care fell somewhat between the two rounds.")`

# Discussion {#sec:s7}

## Interpretation

Three features of care in Indian households stand out once need is held constant. First, women provide `r pct(sh_child, 0)` of childcare and `r pct(sh_adult, 0)` of adult care in the households that need each`r iff(women_dominate && isTRUE(sh_child >= 0.6), paste0(", so the gender division of care is extreme for both, and ", iff(more_gendered_adult, "more so for adults than for children", "somewhat less so for adults than for children"), ". The population gap in care is not an artefact of men's lower exposure to need"), "")`. Second, the need for adult care has costs in women's time that are invisible in population averages because only `r pct(pr_need_adult, 1)` of households report it. For the women in those households, `r iff(emp_cost, "the cost includes paid work as well as free time", iff(is_neg(c_ft) || is_neg(c_sl), "the cost falls more on free time and sleep than on measured paid work", "the cost is not concentrated in any single use of time that can be measured precisely"))`. Third, care follows position. Wives caring for husbands provide `r pct(wsp_r, 0)` of adult care in single-recipient households, daughters-in-law `r pct(dil_r, 0)` and sons `r pct(son_r, 0)`; people aged 60 and above provide `r pct(sh_min_60, 0)`; and men's care `r iff(is_pos(g_nw), "rises", iff(ok(g_nw), "does not rise measurably", "cannot be compared reliably"))` when no woman is present.

The results bear on the competing accounts in the conceptual framework. `r iff(dil_gt_son, "Daughters-in-law provide more of the care of older parents than the sons to whom the obligation is assigned, which comparative advantage alone does not readily explain.", "Sons provide as much care to older parents as daughters-in-law, which leaves more room for explanations based on comparative advantage.")` `r iff(is_pos(g_nw), "Men's care rises when no woman is present, which is consistent with an assignment of care by gender and position in which men's care is a fallback rather than a share", "Men's care does not rise measurably when no woman is present, so the evidence on substitution does not single out an assignment of care by gender and position")` [@kandiyoti1988bargaining; @folbre1994pays]. `r iff(avail_more, "The caregiver-availability answer points the same way: women's care time rises more where a caregiver is reported available, consistent with that caregiver usually being a woman.", "The caregiver-availability answer does not track women's care time closely, so it captures something other than the presence of a woman carer.")`

## Limitations

The design is a single cross-section, and the estimates are conditional associations. Households in which someone needs care differ in age structure, income and health in ways the controls capture only partly, and families may arrange co-residence according to who is able to care, which would make the carers observed in need households more care-oriented than other women. The direction of this bias for the employment estimates is ambiguous: women with weaker labor-market attachment may be selected as carers, which overstates the cost of care, while households may avoid assigning care to women with good jobs, which understates the cost for women in general.

The need measure is coarse. It records neither severity nor type nor the identity of the recipient, and it covers any member aged five and above. The probable-recipient flag is an approximation: it misses recipients who work and did not receive care on the diary day, and it includes members who received medical care for minor conditions. The caregiver-availability question is the household's own judgment and may be answered differently by households with similar capacity.

A single diary day understates the share of people who ever provide care and overstates its intensity among those who report it [@frazis2012think]. Primary-activity minutes understate supervisory and simultaneous care [@folbre2006measuring; @floro1995women]. The responsibility of being on call for a frail relative, which constrains women's options for paid work outside the home, is not measured at all. The estimates should therefore be read as lower bounds on the time constrained by care.

## Policy implications

Long-term care has entered India's policy agenda mainly through the health system and the welfare of older persons [@unfpa2023ageing]. The results suggest that it should also be treated as a question of gender equality and women's employment. Four implications follow, framed by the agenda of recognizing, reducing and redistributing unpaid care [@elson2017recognize; @addati2018care].

*Recognize.* The household care-need questions in the Time Use Survey are a valuable instrument. Adding the identity of the recipient, the type of need and an indicator of severity would allow official statistics to report care time by recipient, and to track how care burdens change as the population ages. Official summaries of unpaid work may consider reporting care of dependent adults separately from childcare.

*Reduce.* Home-based nursing, day-care centers for older and disabled persons, and assistive devices reduce the time that care requires. They should be evaluated not only by their health effects but also by their effects on carers' time and employment, which this survey can measure.

*Redistribute.* `r iff(dil_gt_son, "Daughters-in-law provide more of the care of the old than sons do.", "Sons and daughters-in-law share the care of the old more evenly than norms suggest.")` `r iff(is_pos(g_nw), "Men's care rises when no woman is available, so men can and do care when care is not assigned to a woman.", iff(ok(g_nw), "Men's care stays low even when no woman is available.", ""))` `r iff(women_dominate, "Policies that treat the \"family\" as the provider of long-term care, without specifying who in the family, in practice assign it to women.", "")` Support for carers, such as respite services, carer allowances or leave entitlements in formal employment, should be available to men as well as women, and could be designed to encourage sharing.

*Prepare for older couples.* People who are themselves over 60, often spouses, provide `r pct(sh_min_60, 0)` of adult care in need households. As fertility falls and migration separates generations, more older couples will live alone. Their care capacity is limited by their own health, and they are the group for whom public provision most directly substitutes for family care.

# Conclusion {#sec:s8}

Conditioning on need changes how care in India looks. In households that need care, women provide `r pct(sh_child, 0)` of childcare minutes and `r pct(sh_adult, 0)` of dependent-adult care minutes`r iff(women_dominate, ", so the gender gap in care is not a gap in exposure", "")`. For working-age women, a member who needs special care is associated with `r diff_txt(c_emp)` time in paid work and `r diff_txt(c_ft)` free time. `r iff(wives_dil_main, "Adult care is provided mainly by wives and daughters-in-law", "Adult care is spread across household positions")`, and people aged 60 and above provide `r pct(sh_min_60, 0)` of it. As the population ages, this form of care will grow. `r iff(women_dominate, "Without public provision and a redistribution of care between men and women, most of it will be supplied by women's time.", "How it is divided between women, men and public provision will shape women's paid work and free time.")`
